replying_to: Replying to Batch-Softmax Contrastive Loss for Pairwise Sentence Scoring Tasks
display_title: Official Review of Paper1106 by Reviewer rjYM

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper explores using the InfoNCE contrastive loss or the batch-softmax contrastive loss for sentence pair scoring tasks in NLP. Towards this, the paper uses the BSC loss in a straightforward manner using embeddings obtained from an underlying SBERT model. 2 methods of constructing the batches: one using example-based shuffling via k-means and one using fast-shuffling using superficial attributes are presented. The empirical evaluation is performed on 4 ranking, 2 classification and 1 regression sentence-similarity scoring tasks, and compares the performance of using the BSC loss (and the BSC + MSE loss) compared to only using the MSE loss.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
1) The BSC loss (ranking loss) which accounts for the entire ranking of the example seems like a natural choice for pairwise sentence scoring tasks (especially ranking tasks like QA, retrieval, etc). This loss has manifested itself in several forms already (Eg: in Dense Passage Retrieval, etc), and thus the empirical improvements presented in some hand-selected datasets are natural and unsurprising.

2) The paper presents related work on the batch-contrastive loss along with different viewpoints such as InfoNCE (via Mutual Information maximization) well by the related work section.

Weakness:

1) The problem and motivation for the paper is weak. The introduction does not provide any reason as to why this is an important problem or approach that needs to be considered important by the NLP research community.

2) There is no technical novelty in the approach presented in the paper. It is a straightforward application of an existing famous loss (InfoNCE) for a pairwise sentence scoring task in NLP. Previously, SimCSE (Gao et al, 2021) have explored using the InfoNCE loss for sentence-pair tasks like NLI, etc.

3) The described approach does not explain how to deal with multiple positives per rank (in case a dataset has more than one correct answers for a single question). This is crucial for Question Answering tasks and is a shortcoming of the proposed BSC loss approach in it's current form.

4) The empirical evaluation of the paper is weak and unconvincing:
	- Missing baseline of SimCE (Gao et al, 2021) from the empirical results tables which also uses the Info-NCE loss.
	
	- The datasets considered in this paper are not well indicative, and sometimes not the original splits: for ranking/ answer-sentence selection there are several more challenging and popular datasets like WikiQA, TREC-QA, ASNQ, etc. , the QQP dataset is randomly sub-sampled and the results cannot be directly compared with previous baselines.
	
	-There are no ablations or studies highlighting the empirical benefits of the specific shuffling approaches proposed in the paper w.r.t a random shuffling baseline. This is crucial for justifying the design choice of the batching strategies.


Missing References:

1) COCO-LM: Correcting and Contrasting Text Sequences for Language Model Pretraining, Meng et al, 2021
2) Supervised contrastive learning for pre-trained language model fine-tuning, Gunel et al, 2021
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a straightforward extension of using the batch contrastive loss (InfoNCE) for sentence-pair scoring tasks in NLP. There is very limited technical novelty to the proposed approach. The experiments are performed on hand-selected datasets, with several important ranking QA datasets missing from the evaluation. The results are presented without strong baselines, and without any ablations highlighting the importance of the presented batching strategies.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1106 by Reviewer rjYM

content.title: Response to Reviewer rjYM
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments. Below we address the issues raised:

> *This loss has manifested itself in several forms already (Eg: in Dense Passage Retrieval, etc), and thus the empirical improvements presented in some hand-selected datasets are natural and unsurprising.*

Note that the use of the standard loss formulation might not have resulted in an empirical improvement. We obtained such results after applying all the proposed modifications. These results are presented as “BSC” and “BSC + MSE”, where we additionally applied the regularization of the dot-product matrix diagonal (in tables in Section 3). The exclusion of each of the proposed modifications reduced the final quality in different tasks and datasets.

> *The problem and motivation for the paper is weak. The introduction does not provide any reason as to why this is an important problem or approach that needs to be considered important by the NLP research community.*

In NLP, it is important to obtain representations of sentences for semantic matching tasks, since they can be used for further analysis (e.g., finding the best answer to a question). A popular approach for this is SentenceBERT. SentenceBERT can be trained with different loss functions, and we show that their choice matters. Moreover, we show that it will not be optimal to use the “standard” contrastive loss, and we suggest ways to increase its efficiency. 

We updated the motivation in the introduction, accordingly.

> *There is no technical novelty in the approach presented in the paper. It is a straightforward application of an existing famous loss (InfoNCE) for a pairwise sentence scoring task in NLP. Previously, SimCSE (Gao et al, 2021) have explored using the InfoNCE loss for sentence-pair tasks like NLI, etc.*

We start with the same standard contrastive loss formulation that was used in SimCSE to train models on labeled datasets. The novelty of our approach is that (i) we make the loss symmetric (there are two terms in our loss), and (ii) we investigate new modifications that were not proposed earlier: all of them are described in Section 3. In particular, we propose several approaches to make the batches, we expand the approach to using negative examples, we make the temperature parameter trainable, we consider new ways to do the normalization and the regularization (through the addition of the MSE component). We carry out an ablation study of each of these new modifications on different tasks and datasets in Section 6. We show that together these modifications can improve quality by 10%.


> *The described approach does not explain how to deal with multiple positives per rank (in case a dataset has more than one correct answers for a single question). This is crucial for Question Answering tasks and is a shortcoming of the proposed BSC loss approach in it's current form.*

There is no problem with multiple positives for the BSC loss since the loss learns mutual information [1], that is, the “probability” of presenting a pair in the dataset of positive pairs of examples. This is indicated in Section 3.1. (end of page 3).

> *The empirical evaluation of the paper is weak and unconvincing:*
> *Missing baseline of SimCE (Gao et al, 2021) from the empirical results tables which also uses the Info-NCE loss.*

SimCSE uses a loss formulation, which we took as a basis. We additionally modified this formulation to improve the final quality.

We added results of unsupervised SimCSE, and they are weak, as expected.

> *There are no ablations or studies highlighting the empirical benefits of the specific shuffling approaches proposed in the paper w.r.t a random shuffling baseline. This is crucial for justifying the design choice of the batching strategies.*

We have presented an ablation study for all modifications. In particular, “BSC - random shuffle” in the tables in Section 6 means that we applied the best modification of the BSC loss, but we took a random shuffle (which was used, for example, in SimCSE). Tables 1, 2, 3 (in Section 6) demonstrate that random shuffling consistently yields worse results (up to 3%).

> *Missing References:*
> COCO-LM: Correcting and Contrasting Text Sequences for Language Model Pretraining, Meng et al, 2021
> Supervised contrastive learning for pre-trained language model fine-tuning, Gunel et al, 2021

We have a reference to the paper “Supervised contrastive learning for pre-trained language model fine-tuning”.

We added a reference to COCO-LM.




[1] Michael  Tschannen,  Josip  Djolonga,  Paul  K.  Rubenstein,  Sylvain  Gelly,  and  Mario  Lucic.   On mutual information maximization for representation learning.   In8th International Conferenceon Learning Representations, ICLR 2020, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, April 26-30, 2020

replying_to: Replying to Batch-Softmax Contrastive Loss for Pairwise Sentence Scoring Tasks
display_title: Official Review of Paper1106 by Reviewer 5avs

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposed a loss function called batch-softmax contrastive (BSC) loss for fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained Transformers for pairwise sentence scoring tasks. In detail, a number of variations for the calculation of the loss were studied, including symmetrization, incorporating labeled negatives, aligning scores on the similarity matrix diagonal, normalizing over the batch axis, etc. Experiments were based on various traditional NLP tasks, i.e., classification, regression, and ranking, which verified the superior performance of the BSE loss.
content.main_review:
Overall, this paper provides a clear overview of the variants of contrastive loss. The method is sound, and the paper is easy to read. 

The major concerns are listed as follows.

[Introduction]

1. Many claims are handwaving, lacking necessary supports. For example, there is no reference in the Introduction part, though it is full of strong claims without any evidence. 

 “While a lot of attention has been paid to the architectures, especially for deep learning, there has been less focus on studying loss functions.” 

- This comment is trivial. There are many studies on loss functions, especially in the era of pre-trained language models, where one of the most important research lines is designing effective loss functions.

“loss functions based on similar or on the same ideas were reinvented multiple times under different names.” 

- This is a strong accusation. I would suggest polishing it to be more accurate or providing adequate details. 

“An example of such universal loss function is the batch-softmax contrastive (BSC) loss, which we will discuss below.”

- No detail is provided in the introduction part. It would be better to use a few sentences to indicate why we need BSC

2. The motivation for the BSC loss is not clear. According to the introduction part, would BSC just unify a “universal” name of previous loss functions?

3. “We study the use of a batch-softmax contrastive loss for fine-tuning large-scale transformers to learn better task-specific sentence embeddings for pairwise sentence scoring tasks.”

- How could the BSC loss learn better task-specific sentence embeddings? What kind of knowledge is captured after training with the new method? It would be beneficial to provide examples to demonstrate the motivation and the effects clearly.

[Related Work]

4. The innovation is limited. In the related work part, the discussion of differences with previous studies is too abstract. 

“we will use the ‘modern’ variant of the loss”, “a number of novel and important modifications”. 

- This work reads like a technical report that combines the findings in previous studies. The techniques presented in Section 3 are existing methods, though there is no reference nor discussion of difference with previous work. It is not clear what is new in this work after reading the whole paper. 

5. “While the above-described loss functions have different names, they are all based on similar ideas.”

- As discussed in the related work part, the existing studies would solve different problems with different motivations. If they are really based on similar ideas, why would the authors choose to combine those components, which would result in redundancy?

[Method]

6. “Pointwise approaches for training models for pairwise sentence scoring tasks, such as mean squared error (MSE), are problematic as the loss does not take the relative order into account. For instance, for two pairs with correct target scores (0.4, 0.5), the loss function would equally penalize answers like (0.3, 0.6) and (0.5, 0.4).”

- This is called the negative divergence issue, which has been studied in text generation. I would suggest adding the reference to help readers have a picture of related studies.

[1] LI, Zuchao, et al. Data-dependent Gaussian Prior Objective for Language Generation. In: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). 2019. 

[2] WIETING, John, et al. Beyond BLEU: Training Neural Machine Translation with Semantic Similarity. In: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL). 2019. p. 4344-4355.

7. “We achieve this by fixing the content of the batches at each epoch of the training process.” “To this end, we apply the current model to encode all pairs at each epoch.”

- This method would cause more memory consumption and computation. How about the training efficiency? 

[Experiments]

8. The observations are intuitive and doubtful regarding the generality. The experiments are only conducted on simple NLP tasks, with only a simple backbone model. Besides, the baselines for comparison are either simple or old. If this work aims to survey the loss choices and find the best combination, it would be necessary to use different backbone baselines and compare them with more recent models.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work attempts to combine the variants of contrastive loss for NLP. I am inclined toward rejecting this paper mainly because of unclear motivation, limited innovation, and primitive experiments.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5avs (Part I)
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments. Below we address the issues raised:

> *Many claims are handwaving, lacking necessary supports. For example, there is no reference in the Introduction part, though it is full of strong claims without any evidence.*
>
> “While a lot of attention has been paid to the architectures, especially for deep learning, there has been less focus on studying loss functions.”
>
> *This comment is trivial. There are many studies on loss functions, especially in the era of pre-trained language models, where one of the most important research lines is designing effective loss functions.*
>
> “loss functions based on similar or on the same ideas were reinvented multiple times under different names.”
>
> *This is a strong accusation. I would suggest polishing it to be more accurate or providing adequate details.*
>
> “An example of such universal loss function is the batch-softmax contrastive (BSC) loss, which we will discuss below.”
>
> *No detail is provided in the introduction part. It would be better to use a few sentences to indicate why we need BSC*

What we mean is that similar modifications were proposed in unrelated papers in different fields (CV, NLP, recommendation systems). This is explained in the Related Work section. We updated the introduction.

> *The motivation for the BSC loss is not clear. According to the introduction part, would BSC just unify a “universal” name of previous loss functions?*

We denote by BSC all losses that are based on the idea of contrasting examples in the batch using softmax. The aim of our paper is to identify ways to learn better task-specific embeddings, and we show that this can be done successfully using the BSC loss.

> *How could the BSC loss learn better task-specific sentence embeddings? What kind of knowledge is captured after training with the new method? It would be beneficial to provide examples to demonstrate the motivation and the effects clearly.*

Task-specific sentence embeddings are better if when using them, the model yields better performance for the task. Indeed, we demonstrated that the BSC loss outperforms MSE and the triplet loss. We updated the motivation in the introduction.

> *The innovation is limited. In the related work part, the discussion of differences with previous studies is too abstract.*
> *This work reads like a technical report that combines the findings in previous studies. The techniques presented in Section 3 are existing methods, though there is no reference nor discussion of difference with previous work. It is not clear what is new in this work after reading the whole paper.*

We do not just combine the results of previous studies. We use the best results as a baseline and we introduce 5 novel modifications (all of them described in Section 3). In particular, we propose several approaches to create the batches, we extend the approach to using negative examples, we make the temperature parameter trainable, and we consider new ways of normalization and regularization (through the addition of the MSE component). We carry out an ablation study of each of these modifications on different tasks and datasets in Section 6. We show that together they can improve the performance by 10%.

> *As discussed in the related work part, the existing studies would solve different problems with different motivations. If they are really based on similar ideas, why would the authors choose to combine those components, which would result in redundancy?*

The tasks are different, but they all aim to find similar objects: images, products, users, questions, etc. Temperature and normalization to unit length were proposed in NLP [1]. Then, these modifications were examined in Computer Vision (SimCLR), and subsequently, they were applied in NLP (SimCSE). Thus, we also use a loss formulation with temperature and normalization.

[1] Zhirong Wu, Yuanjun Xiong, S. Yu, and D. Lin.  Unsupervised feature learning via non-parametric instance discrimination. 2018 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 3733–3742, 2018.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5avs (Part II)
content.comment:
> *This method would cause more memory consumption and computation. How about the training efficiency?*

This is an important step if the input data order is fixed and the size of the dataset is small. Our proposed shuffling procedures fix the input data order. For example, in the case of the CQA-B problem, the quality of the model trained with the fixed data order drops by 3% (row “BSC - w/o shuffle”). It becomes even lower than with classical random shuffling, which reduces the quality by 1.5%. This is mentioned in Section 6 CQA-B.

> *The observations are intuitive and doubtful regarding the generality. The experiments are only conducted on simple NLP tasks, with only a simple backbone model. Besides, the baselines for comparison are either simple or old. If this work aims to survey the loss choices and find the best combination, it would be necessary to use different backbone baselines and compare them with more recent models.*

Our goal was to compare the BSC loss to other losses for learning sentence embeddings (MSE, triplet loss, which are used in SBERT). Moreover, we showed the importance of our new modifications compared to standard training with BSC loss, but we do not compare different models.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1106 by Reviewer EYaq

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents batch-softmax contrastive loss which selects hard negatives as in-batch negatives and comparing question to answer only rather than question to question and answer to answer.
Results show that the proposed objective could achieve better performance than baselines in datasets that require semantic similarity.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- S1 - The idea of batch contrastive learning is interesting. Unlike SimCLR (Chen et al., 2020) and SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021), the loss is more focused on sequence classification tasks.
- S2 - The paper is well-written and easy-to-follow.

Weakness and Questions:
- W1 - I think the important baseline is missing. Unsupervised SimCSE can be applied to these datasets since most dataset is based on semantic similarity, not question answering tasks. Since the paper is mentioning that the difference from SimCSE-style loss is not comparing the (q1,q2) and (a1,a2), think the paper can present the performance difference as well. Also, SupCL-seq (Sedghamiz et al., 2021) can be the baseline as well.
- W2 - Such contrastive learning is usually enforcing the semantic similarity of the model. If we use hard negative in terms of semantic similarity (by SBERT), doesn't it potentially harm the performance since it considers true negative examples in the batch as negative instances ? The use of labeled negative examples improve the performance ? What if we sample negatives which are semantically distant ?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper's claim is interesting but still needs more analysis to support the claim.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1106 by Reviewer EYaq

content.title: Response to Reviewer EYaq
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments. Below we address the issues raised:

> *W1 - I think the important baseline is missing. Unsupervised SimCSE can be applied to these datasets since most dataset is based on semantic similarity, not question answering tasks. Since the paper is mentioning that the difference from SimCSE-style loss is not comparing the (q1,q2) and (a1,a2), think the paper can present the performance difference as well. Also, SupCL-seq (Sedghamiz et al., 2021) can be the baseline as well.*

Indeed, SimCSE can be used as an unsupervised baseline. The SimCSE paper describes two approaches to learn embeddings using a contrastive loss: (a) using labeled datasets (such as NLI), and (b) marked up unsupervised via dropout. In either of these approaches, just as in our case, (q1, q2) and (a1, a2) are not compared, since pairs of examples are used for training. Here, the difference with respect to our loss is symmetry: we compare not only qi to all aj, but also ai to all qj in the batch. Note that the goal of SimCSE is to obtain *general* sentence embeddings (and thus, they need to select the best dataset for pretraining), while we aim to obtain *task-specific* embeddings.

We start with the same standard contrastive loss formulation that was used in SimCSE and we train the model on labeled datasets. The novelty of our approach is that (i) we make the loss symmetric (there are two terms in our loss), and (ii) we investigate novel extensions of the loss that were not explored before: all described in Section 3. In particular, we propose novel ways to build the batches, we expand the approach of using negative examples, we make the temperature parameter trainable, and we consider new ways for normalization and regularization (through the addition of the MSE component). We carry out an ablation study of each of these new modifications on different tasks and datasets in Section 6. We show that together they can improve the performance by 10%.

We also added the SimCSE baseline to the results, and it performs much worse than our proposal (which is to be expected, as our embeddings are task-specific, while theirs are not).

> *W2 - Such contrastive learning is usually enforcing the semantic similarity of the model. If we use hard negative in terms of semantic similarity (by SBERT), doesn't it potentially harm the performance since it considers true negative examples in the batch as negative instances ? The use of labeled negative examples improve the performance ? What if we sample negatives which are semantically distant ?*

We explored this issue by applying two modifications, which are described in Sections 3.2 and 3.3. In Section 3.3, we propose a way to use negative examples, and in Section 3.2, we offer options for using these negative examples in a batch. The results for the Antique task (Section 6, Table 1) show that if we use only positive examples without hard negatives (row “BSC - positives”), the quality drops by 2%. If we use only semantically distant negative examples, that is as in the case of random shuffling (which was used, for example, in SimCSE), then the quality of the model can drop substantially (the greatest impact was observed for the CQA tasks: Section 6, Table 2). Our shuffling strategies allow us to control the balance between hard and semantically distant negative examples in the batches.
